nodes.label: Net Income
nodes.formula_human: Pre-Tax Income − Income Tax Expense
nodes.definition: The final, bottom-line profit or loss after all revenues, costs, expenses, non-operating items, and taxes.
nodes.example: Apple FY2024 reported net income of $93.7B, reflecting all costs deducted from $391B in revenue.

playbook.if_increased: (1) revenue growth exceeding cost growth, (2) margin expansion from operating leverage, (3) lower effective tax rate, (4) one-time gains in non-operating items
playbook.if_decreased: (1) revenue decline or deceleration, (2) cost increases outpacing revenue (margin compression), (3) higher effective tax rate, (4) impairment or restructuring charges

comparability.variations: All companies report Net Income. Some report 'Net Income attributable to common shareholders' after deducting minority interest. Non-GAAP measures (Adjusted Net Income) exclude SBC and restructuring.

examples.treatment: Net earnings attributable to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders

nodes.label: Pre-Tax Income (EBT)
nodes.formula_human: Operating Income + Non-Operating Income − Non-Operating Expenses
nodes.definition: Operating Income adjusted for non-operating income and expenses. The basis for calculating income tax expense.
nodes.example: A manufacturer with $10M operating income and $1M interest expense has $9M EBT.
nodes.classification_notes: EBT is the figure to which the effective tax rate is applied. The difference between statutory and effective tax rates is a key analytical metric.

playbook.if_increased: (1) operating income growth, (2) non-operating income gains (investment gains, FX), (3) reduced interest expense from debt paydown, (4) one-time non-operating gains
playbook.if_decreased: (1) operating income decline, (2) increased interest expense from higher debt or rates, (3) impairment or restructuring charges, (4) FX losses

comparability.variations: All companies report pre-tax income. Terminology varies: 'Income before income taxes', 'Earnings before income taxes', 'Income before provision for income taxes'.

examples.treatment: Income before provision for income taxes

nodes.label: Operating Income (EBIT)
nodes.formula_human: Gross Profit − Operating Expenses (Selling + G&A + R&D + D&A)
nodes.definition: Gross Profit minus all operating expenses. Measures profitability from core operations before capital structure and tax effects. The primary measure of operational efficiency.
nodes.example: A SaaS company with 80% gross margins but heavy R&D investment may have slim EBIT.
nodes.classification_notes: Some companies present Operating Income explicitly; others require calculation from disclosed items. Tech companies often show 'Income from Operations'. Manufacturing companies may include or exclude certain restructuring charges depending on materiality.

playbook.if_increased: (1) revenue growth outpacing OpEx growth (operating leverage), (2) gross margin expansion from pricing or COGS efficiency, (3) OpEx reductions from restructuring or efficiency, (4) favorable product mix shift
playbook.if_decreased: (1) revenue decline reducing contribution margin, (2) gross margin compression from input cost increases, (3) OpEx increases from hiring or marketing spend, (4) one-time charges classified as operating

comparability.variations: Most companies report Operating Income or Income from Operations. Some combine it with non-operating items. SaaS companies often highlight non-GAAP operating income excluding SBC.

nodes.label: Gross Profit
nodes.formula_human: Net Revenue − Cost of Goods Sold
nodes.definition: The residual profit after deducting direct costs (COGS) from Net Revenue. Represents the margin available to cover operating expenses, interest, taxes, and generate net income.
nodes.example: A retail company with $500M net revenue and $350M COGS reports $150M gross profit (30% gross margin).
nodes.classification_notes: Gross Profit is not always explicitly reported as a line item. Some companies go directly from Revenue to Operating Income. Financial services companies typically do not report Gross Profit — their equivalent is Net Interest Income or Net Revenue after provisions.

playbook.if_increased: (1) revenue growth outpacing COGS growth, (2) pricing power — price increases not offset by cost increases, (3) favorable product/service mix shift toward higher-margin offerings, (4) cost reduction initiatives in direct costs, (5) operating leverage in cost of revenue
playbook.if_decreased: (1) input cost inflation eroding margins, (2) competitive pricing pressure forcing price reductions, (3) unfavorable mix shift toward lower-margin products, (4) supply chain disruptions, (5) revenue decline without proportional cost reduction

comparability.variations: Most companies report Gross Profit. SaaS companies typically show 70-85% gross margins; manufacturing 25-45%; retail 20-40%. Financial services companies generally do not present Gross Profit.

examples.treatment: Not reported — uses Net Interest Income

nodes.label: Net Revenue
nodes.formula_human: Gross Revenue − Revenue Deductions
nodes.definition: Gross Revenue minus all revenue deductions (returns, discounts, allowances). The top line of the income statement as reported under ASC 606.
nodes.example: A SaaS company with $100M gross revenue and $5M in volume discounts shows $95M net revenue.

playbook.if_increased: (1) customer/unit volume growth, (2) price increases, (3) new product/service launches, (4) expansion into new markets, (5) favorable product mix shift
playbook.if_decreased: (1) customer churn, (2) competitive pricing pressure, (3) market contraction, (4) unfavorable FX impact, (5) loss of key customer

comparability.variations: Some companies report Gross Revenue; most report Net Revenue as the top line per ASC 606. Financial services companies use Net Interest Income instead.

nodes.label: Gross Revenue
nodes.formula_human: Product Revenue + Service Revenue + Other Revenue
nodes.definition: Total revenue recognized before any deductions. Consists of all revenue streams from the company's primary business activities.
nodes.example: A diversified tech company recognizing $80M product revenue + $50M service revenue + $5M other = $135M gross revenue.

playbook.if_increased: (1) growth in product or service revenue streams, (2) new revenue stream added, (3) price increases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) decline in core revenue stream, (2) product discontinuation, (3) competitive losses

comparability.variations: Most companies report Net Revenue, not Gross. Gross Revenue is typically only visible in the revenue footnote or for companies with material deductions.

examples.treatment: Reports gross vs. net revenue for agency vs. merchant

nodes.label: OTHER REVENUE
nodes.definition: Revenue from secondary or ancillary business activities not classified as product or service revenue.
nodes.example: A manufacturer earning rental income from leasing unused factory space.

nodes.label: Franchise Revenue
nodes.definition: Fees paid by franchisees for the right to operate under the company's brand.

nodes.label: Other Operating Revenue
nodes.definition: Catch-all for revenue from incidental operating activities not otherwise classified.

nodes.label: Royalty Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue from licensing intellectual property (patents, trademarks, content) to third parties.

nodes.label: Product Revenue
nodes.formula_human: Finished Goods Sales + Component/Parts Sales + Licensing of Physical Products
nodes.definition: Revenue from the sale of physical goods, recognized at point of transfer of control.
nodes.example: A manufacturer recognizes product revenue when goods ship to customers.
nodes.classification_notes: Product revenue is typically recognized at a point in time when control transfers to the customer (usually upon shipment or delivery, depending on shipping terms). FOB shipping point vs. FOB destination affects the timing of recognition.

playbook.if_increased: (1) unit volume growth from market expansion, (2) price increases on products, (3) new product launches, (4) favorable product mix shift to higher-ASP items, (5) seasonal demand peaks
playbook.if_decreased: (1) competitive market share loss, (2) product obsolescence or lifecycle decline, (3) pricing pressure from competitors, (4) supply chain constraints limiting shipments, (5) channel destocking

comparability.variations: Manufacturing and retail companies report product revenue prominently. Some companies combine product and service revenue into a single 'Net Sales' line. Tech companies may report 'Products' and 'Services' separately.

nodes.label: Component / Parts Sales
nodes.definition: Revenue from selling individual components or spare parts.
nodes.example: An electronics company selling replacement components to repair shops.

nodes.label: Finished Goods Sales
nodes.definition: Revenue from selling completed manufactured products.
nodes.example: An auto manufacturer recognizing revenue from vehicle sales to dealerships.

nodes.label: Licensing of Physical Products
nodes.definition: Revenue from licensing rights to use a physical product design (distinct from software licensing).

nodes.label: RECURRING VS. NON-RECURRING REVENUE
nodes.classification_notes: Not a separate GL account — a classification overlay for analytical purposes.

nodes.label: Service Revenue
nodes.formula_human: Professional Services Revenue + Subscription Revenue + Maintenance & Support Revenue + Usage-Based Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue recognized over time or at completion of a performance obligation for services rendered.
nodes.example: A consulting firm recognizing revenue as hours are worked under a time-and-materials contract.
nodes.classification_notes: Service revenue is recognized over time when the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits (ASC 606-10-25-27). For SaaS, subscription revenue is the dominant sub-component. Professional services may be recognized over time or at a point in time depending on contract terms.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new customer acquisition, (2) price increases on renewals, (3) upsell/cross-sell expanding customer spend, (4) improved retention reducing churn, (5) new service line launch
playbook.if_decreased: (1) customer churn or downgrades, (2) competitive pricing pressure, (3) delayed project starts (professional services), (4) consumption decline (usage-based), (5) contract non-renewals

comparability.variations: SaaS companies report subscription revenue as the primary component. Professional services firms may report consulting revenue separately. Some companies disaggregate by geography rather than service type.

nodes.label: Maintenance & Support Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue from post-sale technical support or maintenance agreements.
nodes.example: Oracle recognizing annual support fees on database licenses.

nodes.label: Professional Services Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue from consulting, advisory, implementation, or other project-based services.
nodes.example: Deloitte recognizing revenue as consulting hours are delivered.

nodes.label: Subscription Revenue
nodes.formula_human: Revenue recognized ratably over subscription periods
nodes.definition: Revenue recognized ratably over a subscription period (monthly/annually). Most common in SaaS.
nodes.example: Salesforce recognizing $10K/month from a $120K annual CRM contract.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new customer acquisition, (2) expansion revenue (upsells/cross-sells), (3) price increases on renewals, (4) lower churn rate
playbook.if_decreased: (1) increased churn/downgrades, (2) slower new logo acquisition, (3) competitive pricing pressure, (4) contract term changes (annual→monthly)

comparability.variations: Some companies split subscription vs. consumption revenue. Others bundle subscription with maintenance/support.

examples.treatment: Included in Intelligent Cloud and Productivity segments

nodes.label: Usage-Based Revenue
nodes.definition: Revenue recognized based on actual consumption or usage (per-API-call, per-GB, per-transaction).
nodes.example: AWS recognizing revenue based on EC2 compute hours consumed each month.

nodes.label: Revenue Deductions
nodes.formula_human: Sales Returns & Allowances + Sales Discounts + Rebates & Credits
nodes.definition: Reductions to Gross Revenue required under ASC 606 to arrive at Net Revenue. These are contra-revenue items (credit-balance offsets to revenue) — they reduce the top line but are not expenses.
nodes.example: A software company reporting $100M gross revenue with $5M in volume discounts shows $95M net revenue.
nodes.classification_notes: Revenue deductions are contra-revenue items with a normal DEBIT balance that offset CREDIT revenue. Under ASC 606, variable consideration (discounts, rebates, returns) must be estimated and deducted from revenue at the time of recognition. Most companies report only Net Revenue, making these deductions visible only in footnotes.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher return rates from quality issues or seasonal patterns, (2) increased promotional discounting, (3) new volume discount tiers triggered by customer growth, (4) channel partner rebate accrual increases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) improved product quality reducing returns, (2) reduced promotional activity, (3) tighter discount policies, (4) shift to less discount-sensitive channels

comparability.variations: Most companies report Net Revenue only; gross-to-net bridge is rarely visible on the face of the P&L. E-commerce and retail companies tend to have higher return rates. SaaS companies typically have minimal deductions.

examples.treatment: Returns netted against revenue; not separately disclosed
Revenue deductions for Medicaid/Medicare rebates disclosed in notes

nodes.label: REBATES & CREDITS
nodes.definition: Post-sale cash payments or credits back to customers tied to cumulative purchase milestones.

nodes.label: Channel / Distributor Rebates
nodes.definition: Rebates paid to distributors or channel partners for hitting sales volume targets.

nodes.label: Customer Loyalty Credits
nodes.definition: Credits issued to customers under loyalty programs redeemable against future purchases.

nodes.label: Contract Rebates & True-ups
nodes.definition: Adjustments to rebate accruals at contract anniversary dates when actual volumes differ from estimates.

nodes.label: SALES DISCOUNTS
nodes.definition: Reductions in the invoice price offered to customers; contra-revenue under ASC 606.

nodes.label: Early Payment / Cash Discounts
nodes.definition: Discounts offered for early payment (e.g., "2/10 net 30" = 2% discount if paid in 10 days).

nodes.label: Promotional Discounts
nodes.definition: Temporary price reductions for marketing promotions or seasonal events.

nodes.label: Volume / Quantity Discounts
nodes.definition: Price reductions given to customers who purchase above threshold quantities.

nodes.label: SALES RETURNS & ALLOWANCES
nodes.definition: Reductions for goods returned by customers or credits granted for defective/damaged goods.

nodes.label: Allowances for Defective Goods
nodes.definition: Credits issued to customers who keep defective goods in lieu of returning them.

nodes.label: Merchandise Returns
nodes.definition: Physical goods returned by customers; reduces revenue and restores inventory.
nodes.example: A retailer processing holiday returns in January.

nodes.label: Reserve for Future Returns
nodes.definition: Estimated future returns accrued at time of revenue recognition per ASC 606.
nodes.example: An e-commerce company accruing a 3% return reserve on all holiday season sales.

nodes.label: COST OF GOODS SOLD (COGS) / COST OF REVENUE
nodes.definition: The direct costs attributable to producing the goods sold or delivering the services rendered. Subtracted from Net Revenue to derive Gross Profit. The line that divides "how much it costs to make the product" from "how much it costs to run the business."
nodes.example: For a car manufacturer, COGS includes steel, assembly labor, and factory overhead. For a SaaS company, COGS includes hosting, infrastructure, and customer support labor.

nodes.label: DIRECT LABOR
nodes.definition: Compensation for employees whose time is directly and exclusively tied to production of the goods sold. Excludes supervisory, administrative, and indirect labor.

nodes.label: BENEFITS — DIRECT LABOR
nodes.definition: Employee benefits costs attributable to direct production workforce.

nodes.label: Health Insurance — Direct
nodes.definition: Employer-paid health insurance premiums for direct labor employees.

nodes.label: Retirement Contributions — Direct
nodes.definition: Employer 401(k) or pension contributions for direct labor employees.

nodes.label: Workers' Compensation — Direct
nodes.definition: Workers' compensation insurance premium attributable to direct production employees.

nodes.label: PAYROLL TAXES — DIRECT
nodes.definition: Employer-paid payroll taxes (FICA, FUTA, SUTA) attributable to direct labor employees.

nodes.label: Employer FICA / Payroll Tax — Direct
nodes.definition: Employer's 7.65% FICA contribution on direct labor wages.

nodes.label: PRODUCTION WAGES
nodes.definition: Gross wages paid to direct production workers.

nodes.label: Production Overtime Pay
nodes.definition: Premium overtime pay (time-and-a-half) for direct production workers exceeding standard hours.

nodes.label: Regular Production Wages
nodes.definition: Standard hourly or salary compensation for direct production employees.
nodes.example: Assembly line workers at an auto plant.

nodes.label: DIRECT MATERIALS
nodes.definition: Raw materials and components that physically become part of the finished product.

nodes.label: FREIGHT-IN / INBOUND SHIPPING
nodes.definition: Transportation costs to bring raw materials and components to the manufacturing facility. COGS item (distinct from freight-out to customers, which is typically Selling Expense).

nodes.label: Inbound Freight & Customs
nodes.definition: Shipping, freight, and import duties on incoming materials.

nodes.label: PACKAGING MATERIALS
nodes.definition: Materials used to package the final product for sale and delivery.

nodes.label: Primary Packaging
nodes.definition: Packaging that directly contains the product (boxes, bottles, blister packs).

nodes.label: Secondary / Shipping Packaging
nodes.definition: Outer packaging for shipping (corrugated boxes, pallets, shrink wrap).

nodes.label: PURCHASED COMPONENTS
nodes.definition: Pre-manufactured parts or sub-assemblies purchased from suppliers and incorporated into the final product.
nodes.example: Batteries purchased by an EV manufacturer; processors purchased by a laptop manufacturer.

nodes.label: OEM Components
nodes.definition: Parts sourced from original equipment manufacturers and used in final assembly.

nodes.label: Sub-Assemblies
nodes.definition: Partially assembled components purchased externally and assembled into the final product.

nodes.label: RAW MATERIALS
nodes.definition: Unprocessed inputs purchased to manufacture the product.
nodes.example: Steel coils for an auto manufacturer; cotton for an apparel company.

nodes.label: Primary Raw Material
nodes.definition: The principal material input (e.g., steel in auto manufacturing, silicon in semiconductors).

nodes.label: Secondary Raw Materials
nodes.definition: Supporting material inputs used in smaller quantities (e.g., lubricants, adhesives).

nodes.label: Raw Material Yield Losses
nodes.definition: Waste or scrap from raw material processing that is a normal and expected part of manufacturing.

nodes.label: INVENTORY ADJUSTMENTS
nodes.definition: Adjustments to the value of inventory that flow through COGS, including the mechanical calculation of goods sold from the inventory account and any write-downs.

nodes.label: Beginning Inventory
nodes.definition: Value of inventory on hand at the start of the accounting period. A component of the COGS formula: COGS = Beginning Inventory + Net Purchases − Ending Inventory.

nodes.label: Ending Inventory
nodes.definition: Value of inventory on hand at end of period. Subtracted in the COGS calculation.

nodes.label: INVENTORY WRITE-DOWNS & OBSOLESCENCE
nodes.definition: Reductions in inventory value below cost, recognized when net realizable value (NRV) is below carrying cost (ASC 330).

nodes.label: Inventory Obsolescence Write-down
nodes.definition: Write-down of slow-moving or obsolete inventory to estimated NRV.
nodes.example: A consumer electronics company writing down last-generation phones when new models launch.

nodes.label: Inventory Shrinkage & Spoilage
nodes.definition: Reduction in inventory due to theft, damage, or (for perishables) spoilage.

nodes.label: Net Purchases
nodes.definition: Total purchases of inventory during the period, net of purchase returns and discounts.

nodes.label: MANUFACTURING OVERHEAD
nodes.definition: Indirect production costs that cannot be directly traced to a specific unit of output but are necessary for manufacturing operations. Allocated to products using a predetermined overhead rate.
nodes.example: Factory rent is the same regardless of units produced, but must be absorbed into product cost.

nodes.label: EQUIPMENT & DEPRECIATION
nodes.definition: Costs associated with production equipment and its depreciation over useful life.

nodes.label: Equipment Maintenance & Service Contracts
nodes.definition: Preventive maintenance and service agreements for production equipment.

nodes.label: Equipment Rental / Leasing
nodes.definition: Lease payments on production equipment (operating lease treatment per ASC 842).

nodes.label: Production Equipment Depreciation
nodes.definition: Straight-line or accelerated depreciation on production machinery and equipment (ASC 360).
nodes.example: A $500K CNC machine depreciated over 10 years = $50K/year in production overhead.

nodes.label: FACILITY COSTS
nodes.definition: Costs of operating the physical manufacturing facility.

nodes.label: Facility Maintenance & Repairs
nodes.definition: Ongoing maintenance and repair of the manufacturing facility (not capital improvements).

nodes.label: Factory Rent / Lease
nodes.definition: Rent or lease payments for manufacturing plant and production facilities.

nodes.label: Factory Utilities
nodes.definition: Electricity, gas, water, and other utilities consumed in manufacturing operations.

nodes.label: INDIRECT LABOR & SUPERVISION
nodes.definition: Labor costs for production support roles that cannot be directly traced to specific products.
nodes.example: A quality control manager who oversees the entire production line is indirect labor.

nodes.label: Indirect Production Labor
nodes.definition: Wages for production support roles (material handlers, janitors, forklift operators).

nodes.label: Production Supervisors & Managers
nodes.definition: Salaries of manufacturing supervisors and plant managers.

nodes.label: Quality Control Personnel
nodes.definition: Compensation for QC inspectors and quality assurance staff embedded in production.

nodes.label: PRODUCTION SUPPLIES
nodes.definition: Consumable materials used in manufacturing that are not incorporated into the final product.
nodes.example: Cutting tools, lubricants, safety equipment, cleaning supplies used on the factory floor.

nodes.label: Factory / Production Supplies
nodes.definition: All consumable supplies used in the manufacturing process that are not direct materials.

nodes.label: SERVICE DELIVERY COSTS
nodes.definition: The direct costs of delivering the service to customers. Analogous to direct materials + manufacturing overhead for product companies, but specific to service/SaaS delivery.
nodes.example: For a SaaS company, service delivery costs are cloud hosting, support labor, and third-party data — not R&D, which belongs in Operating Expenses.

nodes.label: CLOUD INFRASTRUCTURE & HOSTING
nodes.definition: Costs of cloud compute, storage, and networking directly tied to serving customers.
nodes.example: AWS, Azure, or GCP charges that scale with the number of active customers or data volume.

nodes.label: Compute / EC2 / Virtual Machines
nodes.definition: Cloud compute instance costs directly serving the production environment.

nodes.label: Networking & CDN
nodes.definition: Data transfer, bandwidth, and content delivery network costs.

nodes.label: Storage / S3 / Object Storage
nodes.definition: Cloud storage costs for customer data in the production environment.

nodes.label: Third-Party Infrastructure Services
nodes.definition: Managed services (databases, monitoring, security) that directly support production.

nodes.label: CUSTOMER SUPPORT LABOR
nodes.definition: Compensation for support agents who directly resolve customer issues with the product. Post-sale technical support essential to service delivery.
nodes.example: A SaaS help desk team handling customer bugs and onboarding issues.

nodes.label: Payroll Taxes — Support
nodes.definition: Employer payroll taxes attributable to COGS-classified support staff.

nodes.label: Support Staff Wages & Salary
nodes.definition: Gross compensation for customer support representatives in COGS.

nodes.label: Support Tools & Software
nodes.definition: Subscriptions to ticketing, CRM, and support tools used by the support team.

nodes.label: DEVOPS / PLATFORM ENGINEERING
nodes.definition: Engineering labor costs for keeping the production platform running and reliable. Excludes R&D (new feature development).
nodes.example: Engineers maintaining uptime, resolving production incidents, and deploying patches.

nodes.label: DevOps / SRE Wages & Salary
nodes.definition: Compensation for engineers whose primary role is production reliability and operations.

nodes.label: Payroll Taxes & Benefits — DevOps
nodes.definition: Employer payroll taxes and benefits for COGS-classified engineering staff.

nodes.label: PAYMENT PROCESSING & TRANSACTION FEES
nodes.definition: Costs charged by payment processors directly tied to revenue transactions.

nodes.label: Credit Card Processing Fees
nodes.definition: Merchant fees (typically 1.5–3%) charged per customer payment transaction.

nodes.label: Payment Gateway Fees
nodes.definition: Fixed or variable fees charged by payment gateway providers (Stripe, Adyen, etc.).

nodes.label: THIRD-PARTY DATA & LICENSED CONTENT
nodes.definition: Costs of data, APIs, or licensed content embedded in the delivered product.
nodes.example: A financial data platform paying Bloomberg for data incorporated into its product.

nodes.label: API / Integration Fees
nodes.definition: Per-call or subscription fees for third-party APIs essential to product functionality.

nodes.label: Data Provider Fees
nodes.definition: Subscription or usage fees for third-party data incorporated into the product.

nodes.label: Licensed Content Fees
nodes.definition: Royalties or licenses for content (images, media, text) delivered through the product.

nodes.label: Cost of Goods Sold
nodes.formula_human: Direct Materials + Direct Labor + Manufacturing Overhead + Other Direct Costs
nodes.definition: The aggregate cost of goods produced and sold, and services rendered during the reporting period. Includes all direct costs attributable to the production of goods or delivery of services — materials, labor, and allocated overhead.
nodes.example: A manufacturer with $40M in raw materials, $15M direct labor, and $10M factory overhead reports $65M COGS against $100M revenue for a 35% gross margin.
nodes.classification_notes: In SaaS companies, COGS is often labeled 'Cost of Revenue' and includes hosting costs, customer support, and amortization of capitalized software. In professional services, it includes billable labor and direct project costs.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher sales volume driving proportional cost increase, (2) raw material or input cost inflation, (3) supply chain disruptions increasing procurement costs, (4) unfavorable product mix shift toward lower-margin products, (5) manufacturing inefficiency or yield loss
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower sales volume, (2) favorable input cost trends or renegotiated supplier contracts, (3) manufacturing efficiency gains or automation, (4) favorable product mix shift, (5) outsourcing or offshoring production

comparability.variations: Terminology varies significantly by industry: 'Cost of Revenue' (tech/SaaS), 'Cost of Goods Sold' (manufacturing/retail), 'Cost of Services' (professional services). Some companies include D&A in COGS; others report it separately.

examples.treatment: Not applicable — uses interest expense and provisions

nodes.label: Shipping & Handling — Classification Decision
nodes.formula_human: Route to COGS or Selling Expenses based on nature and timing of cost
nodes.definition: A decision node that routes shipping and handling costs to the appropriate parent based on whether the cost is incurred before or after transfer of control to the customer, and whether it represents a separate performance obligation.
nodes.example: An e-commerce company incurs $2M inbound freight (classified as COGS) and $5M outbound shipping to customers (could be COGS as fulfillment cost or Selling Expenses depending on policy election).
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 606, shipping and handling after control transfer may be treated as fulfillment cost (COGS) or separate performance obligation. If treated as fulfillment activity, the cost is accrued when revenue is recognized. Companies must elect and consistently apply a policy. Amazon classifies outbound shipping in COGS; many retailers classify it in Selling Expenses.

decision_criteria.condition: Cost incurred to bring goods to saleable condition (inbound freight, warehousing before sale)
Cost incurred to deliver goods to customers (outbound freight, last-mile delivery)
Shipping charged to customer and recognized as separate performance obligation

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher shipment volumes from revenue growth, (2) carrier rate increases, (3) shift toward faster/premium shipping, (4) fuel surcharges, (5) new geographic markets with higher logistics costs
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower order volumes, (2) renegotiated carrier contracts, (3) logistics optimization (route consolidation), (4) shift toward customer pickup or digital delivery, (5) warehouse network optimization reducing shipping distances

comparability.variations: Classification of shipping costs varies significantly across companies. Some classify all shipping in COGS; others split between COGS (inbound) and Selling (outbound). This creates comparability challenges when analyzing gross margins across companies.

examples.treatment: Outbound shipping in Cost of Sales (COGS), also collects shipping revenue
Distribution costs in Operating, selling, general and administrative
Shipping and handling costs in SG&A
Shipping and handling in Merchandise costs (COGS)

nodes.label: Operating Expenses
nodes.formula_human: Selling Expenses + General & Administrative + Research & Development + Depreciation & Amortization (if reported separately)
nodes.definition: The total of all expenses incurred in the ordinary course of business operations, excluding cost of goods sold. Encompasses selling, general & administrative, R&D, and other operating costs.
nodes.example: A SaaS company with $30M in sales & marketing, $20M G&A, and $25M R&D reports $75M total operating expenses.
nodes.classification_notes: The boundary between COGS and OpEx can be subjective. Companies may classify the same type of expense differently. For example, customer support costs may appear in COGS (Salesforce) or in OpEx (others). D&A may be embedded in COGS and OpEx or reported as a separate line.

playbook.if_increased: (1) headcount growth across sales, G&A, or R&D, (2) increased marketing/advertising spend, (3) new office/facility costs, (4) increased R&D investment for new products, (5) one-time restructuring or litigation charges
playbook.if_decreased: (1) workforce reductions or hiring freezes, (2) cost optimization programs, (3) reduced marketing spend, (4) office consolidation, (5) automation replacing manual processes

comparability.variations: Presentation varies: some companies show a single 'Operating Expenses' line; others break out S&M, G&A, R&D individually. Tech companies typically show more granular breakdowns. Some companies include D&A as a separate OpEx line; others embed it within functional categories.

examples.treatment: Research and development + Marketing and sales + General and administrative
Research and development + Selling, general and administrative
Operating, selling, general and administrative expenses
Research and development + Marketing and sales + General and administrative

nodes.label: Selling Expenses
nodes.formula_human: Sales Force Compensation + Advertising & Marketing + Shipping & Distribution + Other Selling Costs
nodes.definition: All expenses directly related to the selling effort — compensation for sales teams, advertising, marketing campaigns, trade shows, shipping to customers, and related costs.
nodes.example: A consumer products company spending $15M on sales team compensation, $10M on advertising, and $3M on distribution reports $28M in selling expenses.
nodes.classification_notes: Many companies combine Selling and G&A into 'SG&A' as a single line item. Tech/SaaS companies often label this 'Sales and Marketing' or 'Marketing and Sales'. The split between selling vs. G&A can be discretionary.

playbook.if_increased: (1) sales team expansion or higher commissions from strong revenue, (2) increased marketing/advertising campaigns, (3) new market entry requiring go-to-market spend, (4) trade show or event-heavy quarter, (5) customer acquisition cost increases
playbook.if_decreased: (1) sales team reductions, (2) reduced advertising spend, (3) shift to lower-cost digital channels, (4) improved sales efficiency (higher revenue per rep), (5) market exit or product line discontinuation

comparability.variations: Reporting varies significantly: some companies present 'Sales and Marketing' as one line; others split selling from marketing; many combine into 'SG&A'. SaaS companies often have selling expenses as 40-60% of revenue in growth phase.

nodes.label: ADVERTISING & MARKETING
nodes.definition: Paid media and brand-building expenditures designed to generate demand.

nodes.label: Brand Sponsorships & Events
nodes.definition: Sponsorship of events, conferences, or organizations for brand visibility.

nodes.label: Content Marketing & SEO
nodes.definition: Production of content (blogs, videos, whitepapers) and SEO optimization spend.

nodes.label: Digital Advertising
nodes.definition: Paid search (Google Ads, Bing), social media ads (Meta, LinkedIn, Twitter/X), display, and programmatic advertising.
nodes.example: A DTC brand spending $2M/month on Meta and Google ads.

nodes.label: Marketing Agency Fees
nodes.definition: Retainer or project fees paid to advertising and marketing agencies.

nodes.label: Marketing Software & Tools
nodes.definition: Subscriptions to marketing automation, analytics, and CRM platforms (HubSpot, Marketo, etc.).

nodes.label: Traditional / Offline Advertising
nodes.definition: TV, radio, print, billboard, and direct mail advertising.

nodes.label: CUSTOMER ACQUISITION & DEMAND GEN
nodes.definition: Direct costs of acquiring new customers outside of advertising (partnerships, trials, referrals).

nodes.label: Free Trial / Demo Costs
nodes.definition: Costs of providing free trials or demos (infrastructure, support, sales engineering time).

nodes.label: Referral & Affiliate Fees
nodes.definition: Fees paid to referral partners or affiliates for new customer introductions.

nodes.label: SALES FORCE COMPENSATION
nodes.definition: All compensation for the sales team, including direct and indirect selling costs.

nodes.label: Payroll Taxes — Sales
nodes.definition: Employer payroll taxes attributable to sales compensation.

nodes.label: Sales Benefits
nodes.definition: Health insurance, retirement, and other benefits for sales employees.

nodes.label: Sales Bonuses & SPIFs
nodes.definition: Non-commission variable pay (quotas bonuses, sales performance incentive funds for specific product pushes).

nodes.label: Sales Commissions
nodes.formula_human: Commission rate × qualifying sales or bookings
nodes.definition: Variable compensation paid to sales personnel based on closed deals, bookings, or revenue targets. Under ASC 340-40, incremental costs of obtaining a contract (including commissions) may be capitalized and amortized over the expected customer benefit period if the amortization period exceeds one year.
nodes.example: A SaaS company paying 10% first-year commission on a $500K ACV deal recognizes $50K commission expense (or capitalizes and amortizes over 3-year expected customer life at ~$16.7K/year).
nodes.classification_notes: Under ASC 340-40, commissions that are incremental costs of obtaining a contract must be capitalized if the expected amortization period exceeds one year. Companies may use a practical expedient to expense commissions as incurred if the amortization period is one year or less. Capitalized commissions are amortized on a systematic basis consistent with the pattern of transfer of goods/services. Renewal commissions at lower rates may be treated differently from new-deal commissions.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher bookings/revenue driving proportional commission payouts, (2) sales team expansion, (3) commission plan changes (higher rates or accelerators), (4) large enterprise deal closings with premium commission rates, (5) shift in mix toward new business vs. renewals (new typically pays higher)
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower bookings volume, (2) sales team attrition not backfilled, (3) commission plan restructuring (lower rates), (4) shift toward renewal-heavy mix (lower commission rates), (5) increased use of channel partners (partner margins vs. direct commissions)

comparability.variations: Some companies report commissions within Sales & Marketing; others embed them in SG&A. ASC 340-40 capitalization creates timing differences — a company capitalizing commissions shows lower current-period expense but carries a deferred asset on the balance sheet.

examples.treatment: Capitalized as 'Deferred commissions' on balance sheet, amortized over ~5 years in Marketing and Sales
Not separately disclosed — embedded in SG&A (primarily retail and online sales, minimal traditional commission structure)
Capitalized per ASC 340-40, amortized in Selling, general and administrative over estimated customer benefit period

nodes.label: Sales Salaries & Base Pay
nodes.definition: Fixed salary component for sales representatives and account executives.

nodes.label: SHIPPING & DISTRIBUTION
nodes.definition: Costs of delivering goods to customers (freight-out). SELLING expense — distinct from freight-in on materials, which is COGS.

nodes.label: Distribution Center Costs
nodes.definition: Operating costs of distribution centers handling finished goods awaiting delivery.

nodes.label: Outbound Freight & Shipping
nodes.definition: Third-party shipping costs to deliver products to customers.

nodes.label: TRADE SHOWS & SALES EVENTS
nodes.definition: Costs of exhibiting at or hosting trade shows, industry conferences, and sales events.
nodes.example: A B2B software company spending $300K on a booth at Dreamforce.

nodes.label: Booth / Exhibit Space
nodes.definition: Rental fees for trade show floor space.

nodes.label: Event Travel & Entertainment
nodes.definition: Travel, lodging, and entertainment for sales staff attending events.

nodes.label: Trade Show Materials & Setup
nodes.definition: Display materials, signage, collateral, and setup/teardown costs.

nodes.label: General & Administrative Expenses (G&A)
nodes.formula_human: Executive Compensation + HR + Finance & Accounting + Legal + Office & Facilities + IT + General Corporate Overhead
nodes.formula_machine: fintree:ExecutiveManagementCompensation + fintree:HumanResources + fintree:FinanceAccounting + fintree:LegalCompliance + fintree:OfficeFacilitiesCorporate + fintree:InformationTechnology + fintree:GeneralCorporateOverhead
nodes.definition: The overhead costs of running the corporate organization — all costs not directly attributable to selling or producing. Sometimes called 'corporate overhead.' Includes executive management, finance, legal, HR, IT, and office operations.
nodes.example: Amazon describes G&A as 'payroll and related expenses; facilities and equipment; professional fees; and other general corporate costs for accounting, finance, tax, legal, and HR.'
nodes.classification_notes: Many companies combine G&A with Selling Expenses into 'SG&A' (Selling, General and Administrative). The split between selling and G&A is discretionary. Stock-based compensation for G&A employees is typically included here.

playbook.if_increased: (1) executive hiring or compensation increases, (2) office space expansion, (3) increased legal/compliance costs, (4) new ERP or IT system implementations, (5) audit fee increases for public company requirements
playbook.if_decreased: (1) headcount reductions in corporate functions, (2) office consolidation or shift to remote work, (3) renegotiated vendor contracts, (4) automation of back-office processes, (5) outsourcing of functions

comparability.variations: Reporting of G&A varies significantly. Some companies report SG&A combined; others break out S&M and G&A separately. Tech companies often have high G&A due to stock-based compensation.

nodes.label: EXECUTIVE & MANAGEMENT COMPENSATION
nodes.definition: Compensation for C-suite executives and senior management whose roles span the entire business rather than a single function.

nodes.label: Executive Benefits & Perquisites
nodes.definition: Benefits specific to executive roles (supplemental insurance, car allowances, housing, etc.).

nodes.label: Executive Bonuses & Incentive Pay
nodes.definition: Annual performance bonuses for executives tied to company-wide metrics.

nodes.label: Executive Salaries (CEO, CFO, COO, etc.)
nodes.definition: Base salary for top executive officers.

nodes.label: Stock-Based Compensation — G&A
nodes.definition: Expense recognized for equity awards (RSUs, stock options) granted to G&A employees (ASC 718).
nodes.example: A $1M RSU grant vesting over 4 years = $250K/year SBC expense in G&A.

nodes.label: FINANCE & ACCOUNTING
nodes.definition: Costs of the finance and accounting function, including internal staff and external professional services.

nodes.label: Accounting Software & ERP
nodes.definition: Subscriptions to ERP and accounting platforms (SAP, Oracle, NetSuite, QuickBooks).

nodes.label: External Audit Fees
nodes.definition: Fees paid to public accounting firms for the annual financial statement audit.
nodes.example: A mid-cap public company paying $1.5M/year to a Big 4 firm for its annual audit.

nodes.label: Finance & Accounting Staff Compensation
nodes.definition: Salaries, payroll taxes, and benefits for CFO, controllers, accountants, FP&A staff.

nodes.label: Financial Reporting Costs
nodes.definition: Costs of external financial reporting, XBRL tagging, and SEC filing services.

nodes.label: Tax Advisory & Compliance Fees
nodes.definition: Fees for external tax preparation, planning, and compliance services.

nodes.label: GENERAL CORPORATE OVERHEAD
nodes.definition: Miscellaneous G&A costs not classified into the above sub-categories.

nodes.label: Business Travel & Entertainment
nodes.definition: Corporate travel, lodging, and business entertainment for non-sales employees.

nodes.label: Meals & Entertainment
nodes.definition: Business meals with clients, staff meals, and entertainment (subject to IRS 50% deductibility limit).

nodes.label: Miscellaneous G&A
nodes.definition: Catch-all for minor G&A costs not warranting a separate line item.

nodes.label: Subscriptions & Publications
nodes.definition: Industry publications, research subscriptions, and news services for corporate management.

nodes.label: HUMAN RESOURCES
nodes.definition: Costs of the HR function — recruiting, training, employee relations, and HR administration.

nodes.label: Employee Training & Development
nodes.definition: Costs of training programs, workshops, online learning platforms (LinkedIn Learning, Udemy), and conferences for professional development.

nodes.label: HR Staff Compensation
nodes.definition: Salaries, payroll taxes, and benefits for the HR department.

nodes.label: HRIS & HR Software
nodes.definition: Subscriptions to HR information systems, payroll software, and benefits administration platforms (Workday, ADP, Rippling).

nodes.label: Recruiting & Hiring Costs
nodes.definition: External recruiter fees (typically 15–25% of first-year salary), job board postings, background checks.
nodes.example: A company paying a $30K recruiter fee to fill a $120K engineering role.

nodes.label: INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (IT)
nodes.definition: Costs of corporate IT infrastructure and systems, excluding software used in the production environment (which is COGS for SaaS).
nodes.example: A company's internal email servers, corporate laptops, and business intelligence tools are G&A IT.

nodes.label: Cybersecurity & Compliance Software
nodes.definition: Security software, penetration testing, and compliance tooling for corporate systems.

nodes.label: Hardware & Equipment — Corporate
nodes.definition: Corporate laptops, servers, networking equipment (either expensed if below capitalization threshold or depreciated).

nodes.label: IT Infrastructure & Networking
nodes.definition: Corporate network infrastructure, VPN, cybersecurity tools, and cloud services for internal operations.

nodes.label: IT Staff Compensation
nodes.definition: Salaries and benefits for internal IT support and systems staff.

nodes.label: Software Subscriptions — Corporate
nodes.definition: Business software subscriptions for productivity, communication, and corporate operations (Microsoft 365, Slack, Zoom, Salesforce for internal use).

nodes.label: LEGAL & COMPLIANCE
nodes.definition: Costs of legal counsel, regulatory compliance, and corporate governance.

nodes.label: D&O and Other Corporate Insurance
nodes.definition: Directors & Officers liability insurance and other corporate insurance policies.
nodes.classification_notes: General liability and property insurance specific to production facilities is Manufacturing Overhead; this is corporate-level insurance.

nodes.label: External Legal Fees — General Corporate
nodes.definition: Retainer and hourly fees for corporate legal counsel (contracts, corporate governance, employment law).

nodes.label: External Legal Fees — Litigation
nodes.definition: Fees for defending or prosecuting lawsuits (disclosed separately if material per Reg S-X).

nodes.label: Intellectual Property (Patent / Trademark)
nodes.definition: Patent filing, maintenance, and trademark registration fees.

nodes.label: Regulatory & Compliance Fees
nodes.definition: Costs of regulatory filings, compliance programs, and government fees.

nodes.label: OFFICE & FACILITIES — CORPORATE
nodes.definition: Costs of maintaining corporate office space and facilities (excludes manufacturing/production facilities, which are Manufacturing Overhead).

nodes.label: Corporate Depreciation — Buildings & Fixtures
nodes.definition: Depreciation on owned corporate buildings, leasehold improvements, and office fixtures (ASC 360).

nodes.label: Office Equipment & Supplies
nodes.definition: Consumable office supplies, furniture, and minor equipment not capitalized.

nodes.label: Office Maintenance & Janitorial
nodes.definition: Ongoing maintenance, cleaning, and facility management for corporate offices.

nodes.label: Office Rent / Lease
nodes.definition: Lease payments for corporate office space (operating lease per ASC 842).

nodes.label: Office Utilities
nodes.definition: Electricity, HVAC, water, and other utilities for corporate offices.

nodes.label: Research & Development (R&D)
nodes.formula_human: R&D Personnel + R&D Materials & Supplies + R&D Equipment & Facilities + External/Contract Research
nodes.definition: Costs incurred to discover new knowledge or create new products, processes, or technologies. Expensed as incurred under ASC 730 (with certain software development costs capitalized under ASC 350-40). Note: As of 2022, IRC Section 174 requires R&D to be capitalized and amortized for TAX purposes, but it continues to be expensed for GAAP purposes.
nodes.example: Google's 'Other Bets' research projects and core search algorithm development both flow through R&D.
nodes.classification_notes: R&D is expensed as incurred for GAAP (ASC 730). Software development costs may be capitalized once technological feasibility is established (ASC 985-20) or during application development stage for internal-use software (ASC 350-40). Stock-based compensation for R&D employees is included here.

playbook.if_increased: (1) engineering hiring for new product development, (2) increased cloud compute for ML/AI training, (3) new R&D facility or lab investment, (4) clinical trial costs (pharma), (5) strategic pivot requiring new technology
playbook.if_decreased: (1) R&D headcount reductions, (2) project completions or cancellations, (3) shift from internal to acquired technology, (4) R&D tax credit offset (if shown as reduction), (5) capitalization of software development costs

comparability.variations: Tech companies typically report R&D as a separate line item and it represents 15-25% of revenue. Pharma companies may have R&D exceeding revenue for pre-commercial-stage companies. Manufacturing companies may embed R&D within SG&A.

nodes.label: EXTERNAL / CONTRACT RESEARCH
nodes.definition: Payments to third parties for research conducted on the company's behalf.

nodes.label: Contract Research Organizations (CRO)
nodes.definition: Fees for external research firms or CROs conducting qualifying research.
nodes.example: A pharma company paying a CRO for clinical trial management.

nodes.label: University Research Grants & Partnerships
nodes.definition: Funding provided to academic institutions for collaborative R&D.

nodes.label: R&D Tax Credit Offset
nodes.definition: Where companies offset R&D expense with R&D tax credits on the P&L. Less common; credit usually flows through tax expense, but some companies show it as an R&D offset.

nodes.label: R&D EQUIPMENT & FACILITIES
nodes.definition: Equipment and facility costs dedicated to R&D activities.

nodes.label: R&D Cloud Compute
nodes.definition: Cloud computing costs for R&D model training, testing, and experimentation (separate from production infrastructure in COGS).
nodes.example: An AI company's GPU compute costs for training new models before deployment.

nodes.label: R&D Equipment Depreciation
nodes.definition: Depreciation on equipment used exclusively for research and development.

nodes.label: R&D Lab / Office Space
nodes.definition: Allocated or dedicated facility costs for research labs and development offices.

nodes.label: R&D MATERIALS & SUPPLIES
nodes.definition: Consumable materials, supplies, and prototype components used in R&D activities.

nodes.label: Laboratory & Research Supplies
nodes.definition: Consumable lab supplies, chemicals, reagents, and research materials.
nodes.example: A pharmaceutical company's lab chemicals used in drug discovery.

nodes.label: Prototype Materials
nodes.definition: Materials used to build product prototypes during development.

nodes.label: R&D Software & Development Tools
nodes.definition: Licenses for development environments, IDEs, testing tools, and research software.

nodes.label: R&D PERSONNEL
nodes.definition: Compensation for employees engaged in qualifying research and development activities.

nodes.label: Payroll Taxes — R&D
nodes.definition: Employer payroll taxes attributable to R&D workforce.

nodes.label: R&D Benefits
nodes.definition: Health insurance, retirement, and benefits for R&D employees.

nodes.label: R&D Bonuses & Incentive Pay
nodes.definition: Performance bonuses for R&D staff tied to innovation milestones.

nodes.label: R&D Salaries & Wages
nodes.definition: Base salary and wages for scientists, engineers, and developers engaged in R&D.

nodes.label: Stock-Based Compensation — R&D
nodes.definition: Equity award expense for R&D employees (ASC 718).

nodes.label: Depreciation & Amortization (D&A)
nodes.formula_human: Depreciation of PP&E + Amortization of Intangible Assets
nodes.definition: The non-cash allocation of the cost of long-lived assets over their useful lives. Often embedded within COGS, SG&A, or R&D rather than shown as a separate line item. When disclosed separately, it represents total D&A from all functions.
nodes.example: A manufacturing company with $500M in PP&E and $200M in acquired intangibles may record $80M in annual D&A.
nodes.classification_notes: Whether D&A is shown separately or embedded within functional categories is a PRESENTATION choice -- the underlying sub-items are the same. For EBITDA calculations, total D&A must be gathered from the cash flow statement or notes if not separately presented on the income statement.

playbook.if_increased: (1) new capital expenditures entering depreciable base, (2) acquisitions adding intangible assets, (3) change in depreciation method or useful life estimates, (4) accelerated depreciation from impairment indicators
playbook.if_decreased: (1) assets reaching end of useful life (fully depreciated), (2) asset disposals or sales, (3) change to longer useful life estimates, (4) reduced capital spending in prior years

comparability.variations: D&A presentation varies significantly. Capital-intensive companies (manufacturing, telecom) show large D&A. Asset-light companies (SaaS, consulting) have minimal depreciation but may have significant amortization from acquisitions.

examples.treatment: Depreciation and amortization (separate line, very large)
Embedded in cost of revenues and operating expenses; total in cash flow statement
Depreciation and amortization shown in operating expenses

nodes.label: AMORTIZATION OF INTANGIBLE ASSETS
nodes.definition: Allocation of acquired intangible asset cost over useful life (ASC 350). Applies to acquired assets; internally developed intangibles are generally expensed as incurred.

nodes.label: Capitalized Software Amortization
nodes.definition: Amortization of internally capitalized software development costs per ASC 350-40 (application development stage only).

nodes.label: Customer Relationship Amortization
nodes.definition: Amortization of customer relationship intangibles acquired in a business combination.
nodes.example: A company acquired for $100M with $20M attributed to customer relationships, amortized over 7 years.

nodes.label: Right-of-Use Asset Amortization
nodes.definition: Amortization of finance lease right-of-use assets (ASC 842).

nodes.label: Technology / IP Amortization
nodes.definition: Amortization of acquired patents, trademarks, and developed technology intangibles.

nodes.label: Trade Name Amortization
nodes.definition: Amortization of acquired trade names with finite useful lives.

nodes.label: DEPRECIATION OF PROPERTY, PLANT & EQUIPMENT
nodes.definition: Allocation of PP&E cost over its useful life (ASC 360). Method: straight-line, declining balance, or units-of-production.

nodes.label: Building & Improvement Depreciation
nodes.definition: Depreciation on owned buildings and leasehold improvements.

nodes.label: Furniture & Fixtures Depreciation
nodes.definition: Depreciation on office furniture, fixtures, and minor tangible assets.

nodes.label: Machinery & Equipment Depreciation
nodes.definition: Depreciation on production machinery, manufacturing equipment, and heavy machinery.

nodes.label: Vehicles Depreciation
nodes.definition: Depreciation on company-owned vehicles.

nodes.label: Non-Operating Income & Expenses
nodes.formula_human: Non-Operating Income − Non-Operating Expenses
nodes.definition: Income and expenses that arise from activities outside the company's core operations. These items fall BELOW the Operating Income (EBIT) line. Including them in operating income would distort the measure of core operational performance. Key analytical principle: separating operating from non-operating items allows analysts to assess sustainable earnings vs. one-time or financing-driven items.
nodes.example: Interest expense is non-operating because it reflects financing decisions (how much debt the company has), not operating efficiency.
nodes.classification_notes: Non-operating items bridge the gap between Operating Income and Pre-Tax Income. The net amount can be positive (net non-operating income) or negative (net non-operating expense). Financial services companies have a different operating/non-operating boundary since interest income is part of core operations for banks.

playbook.if_increased: (1) investment gains or higher interest income on cash balances, (2) gains on asset disposals, (3) favorable FX movements, (4) reduced debt lowering interest expense
playbook.if_decreased: (1) higher interest expense from new debt or rising rates, (2) impairment charges on investments, (3) restructuring charges classified below EBIT, (4) unfavorable FX movements, (5) loss on asset disposals

comparability.variations: Presentation varies widely. Some companies show 'Other income (expense), net' as a single line. Others break out interest expense, interest income, and other items separately. Financial services companies treat interest as operating.

examples.treatment: Interest income, Interest expense, Other income (expense) — shown separately

nodes.label: NON-OPERATING INCOME
nodes.definition: Gains and income from activities outside core operations.

nodes.label: Dividend Income
nodes.definition: Dividends received from equity investments (typically minority stakes, not consolidated subsidiaries).

nodes.label: Gain on Foreign Exchange
nodes.definition: Realized and unrealized gains from currency rate movements on foreign-denominated assets/liabilities.

nodes.label: Gain on Investments
nodes.definition: Mark-to-market gains or realized gains from equity investments.

nodes.label: Gain on Sale of Assets
nodes.definition: Proceeds in excess of book value from selling property, equipment, or investments.

nodes.label: Interest Income
nodes.definition: Interest earned on cash deposits, money market funds, and fixed income investments.
nodes.example: Apple earning billions in interest income on its cash/investment portfolio.

nodes.label: Other Non-Operating Income
nodes.definition: Catch-all for non-operating income items not classified above (sublease income, government grants, etc.).

nodes.label: NON-OPERATING EXPENSES
nodes.definition: Costs outside core operations — primarily financing costs and exceptional charges.

nodes.label: Foreign Exchange Loss
nodes.definition: Realized and unrealized losses from adverse currency movements on foreign-denominated items.
nodes.example: A US company with euro-denominated receivables loses value when the euro weakens against the dollar.

nodes.label: INTEREST EXPENSE
nodes.definition: The cost of borrowed capital — interest payments on debt instruments. The primary non-operating expense for most companies. Reflects financing decisions, not operational performance.

nodes.label: Amortization of Debt Issuance Costs
nodes.definition: Amortization of financing fees paid to issue debt instruments (treated as an interest expense component under ASC 835).

nodes.label: Finance Lease Interest
nodes.definition: Interest component of finance lease payments (ASC 842) — treated as interest expense on the P&L.

nodes.label: Interest on Long-Term Debt
nodes.definition: Interest on bonds, term loans, and other long-term borrowings.
nodes.example: A company with $500M in bonds at 5% interest records $25M/year interest expense.

nodes.label: Interest on Revolving Credit Facility
nodes.definition: Interest on drawn balances of revolving credit lines.

nodes.label: Impairment Charges
nodes.definition: Write-down of long-lived assets or goodwill when carrying value exceeds recoverable amount (ASC 350, ASC 360).
nodes.example: A media company writing down acquired goodwill after a business unit underperforms.

nodes.label: Loss on Sale of Assets
nodes.definition: Book value in excess of proceeds when selling property, equipment, or investments below carrying value.

nodes.label: Other Non-Operating Expenses
nodes.definition: Miscellaneous non-operating charges — legal settlements, regulatory fines, and other exceptional costs.

nodes.label: Restructuring Charges
nodes.definition: Costs of significant reorganization — severance, facility closures, contract terminations. Non-recurring. Required to be disclosed separately when material.
nodes.example: A company announcing layoffs of 10% of its workforce accrues severance as a restructuring charge.

nodes.label: Income Tax Expense
nodes.formula_human: Current Tax Expense + Deferred Tax Expense (Benefit)
nodes.definition: Total income tax charge on the income statement, comprising current and deferred tax components. Governed by ASC Topic 740. May differ significantly from cash taxes paid due to deferred tax mechanisms.
nodes.example: A company with $100M pre-tax income and a 21% US corporate rate records approximately $21M income tax expense, adjusted for deferred items.
nodes.classification_notes: Income tax expense is the last deduction before Net Income. The effective tax rate (tax expense / pre-tax income) is a key metric. Differences from the statutory 21% rate arise from state taxes, international operations, R&D credits, and permanent differences.

playbook.if_increased: (1) higher pre-tax income, (2) unfavorable discrete tax items (audit settlements, valuation allowance increases), (3) shift in geographic income mix to higher-tax jurisdictions, (4) expiration of tax credits
playbook.if_decreased: (1) lower pre-tax income, (2) favorable discrete items (R&D credits, stock option windfalls), (3) shift to lower-tax jurisdictions, (4) new tax incentives or credits

comparability.variations: All companies report income tax expense. Key variation is the effective tax rate, which varies widely by company based on geographic mix, credits, and incentives. Some companies report 'Provision for income taxes' vs. 'Income tax expense'.

examples.treatment: Provision for income taxes (~15% ETR due to Ireland structure)
Provision for income taxes (variable ETR due to SBC deductions)
Income taxes (high ETR due to domestic income concentration)

nodes.label: CURRENT TAX EXPENSE
nodes.definition: The income tax payable to tax authorities for the current period based on taxable income. Computed using the applicable statutory tax rates applied to taxable income per the tax return.

nodes.label: Federal Income Tax — Current
nodes.definition: US federal corporate income tax due for the current year (21% flat rate for corporations as of 2026).

nodes.label: Foreign Income Tax — Current
nodes.definition: Income taxes payable in foreign jurisdictions on income earned outside the US.

nodes.label: State & Local Income Tax — Current
nodes.definition: State and local corporate income taxes due for the current period. Rates vary by jurisdiction.

nodes.label: DEFERRED TAX EXPENSE (BENEFIT)
nodes.definition: The change in deferred tax liabilities and assets arising from temporary differences between GAAP book income and taxable income (ASC 740). When GAAP income exceeds taxable income, a deferred tax liability arises (more tax will be paid later); when taxable income exceeds GAAP income, a deferred tax asset arises.
nodes.example: A company using accelerated depreciation for taxes but straight-line for GAAP recognizes a deferred tax liability because it's paying less tax now (will pay more later).

nodes.label: Deferred Tax Benefit — NOL Carryforward
nodes.definition: Deferred tax asset recognized for net operating loss carryforwards expected to reduce future taxes.
nodes.example: A startup with cumulative losses records a DTA if it expects future profitability to use the NOLs.

nodes.label: Deferred Tax Expense — Depreciation Timing
nodes.definition: Deferred tax arising from different depreciation methods for book vs. tax (most common source).

nodes.label: Other Deferred Tax Items
nodes.definition: Deferred taxes from revenue recognition timing, stock compensation, warranty reserves, and other temporary differences.

nodes.label: BELOW-THE-LINE ITEMS
nodes.definition: Items reported AFTER Net Income from continuing operations, required to be presented separately by GAAP (ASC 205) because they relate to discontinued or extraordinary activities. Including these in operating results would distort the assessment of ongoing business performance.

nodes.label: DISCONTINUED OPERATIONS
nodes.definition: Results of a component of the business that has been disposed of or classified as held-for-sale and represents a separate major line of business or geographic area (ASC 230-20). Shown net of tax.
nodes.example: GE's sale of its financial services division created discontinued operations reporting.

nodes.label: Expenses — Discontinued Operations
nodes.definition: Operating costs attributable to the discontinued business component.

nodes.label: Gain / Loss on Disposal
nodes.definition: The net gain or loss recognized upon actual or expected disposal of the discontinued component.

nodes.label: Revenue — Discontinued Operations
nodes.definition: Revenue attributable to the discontinued business component, shown separately.

nodes.label: EXTRAORDINARY ITEMS
nodes.definition: Under US GAAP (post-ASU 2015-01), extraordinary items as a separate classification were eliminated. However, legacy filings and certain context (e.g., insurance proceeds from natural disasters) still use this nomenclature. Retained here for historical reference and AI context.

nodes.label: Legacy Extraordinary Items
nodes.definition: Pre-2015 classification for unusual and infrequent items. No longer a separate GAAP category; unusual/infrequent items are now disclosed within continuing operations.

nodes.label: CUMULATIVE EFFECT OF ACCOUNTING CHANGES
nodes.definition: The catch-up adjustment when a company changes an accounting principle (ASC 250). Recorded in the period of change, net of tax, as a direct adjustment to opening retained earnings (most changes) or as a separate income statement line for certain changes.

nodes.label: Cumulative Effect of Principle Change
nodes.definition: One-time P&L impact from the transition to a new accounting standard (e.g., adoption of ASC 842 lease accounting).
